title: Numbered list starts at the wrong number in Word on Mac: how to fix it
metaTitle: Numbered list starts at wrong number in Word on Mac: fix
description: A numbered list starts at the wrong number in Word on Mac? Restart it with Restart at 1, nest it under a heading, or use the Google Docs and Pages fixes.

intro: A numbered list starts at the wrong number in Word when it shares a count with an earlier list in the same document. On Mac, right-click the number where the count should begin and choose Restart at 1. If that does nothing, the list needs a structural fix. This page covers both, plus the Google Docs and Pages routes.
tldr: Right-click the wrong number and choose Restart at 1 in Word for Mac. Microsoft's help page gives this as the standard fix.
If Restart at 1 does nothing, nest the list under a Level 1 heading or Body Text paragraph.
Typed numbers never restart on their own. Delete them and reapply list formatting.
Google Docs uses Format > Bullets & numbering > List options. Pages has no documented restart option in its current guide.
The Word steps come from Microsoft's help page, which does not name Mac, so check the menu names on your version.

blocks.text: Here is what it looks like. You type a list of steps, then add a second list further down. Word numbers the second list as if it carries on from the first. The count begins at a number you did not pick, and every item after it is off by the same amount. The words are fine. Only the numbers are wrong. You see this in manuals, reports, grant forms and course notes, anywhere a document has more than one numbered list.
Spot the cause before you change anything

Start by checking what kind of number you are looking at. Click the number and see whether it acts like list formatting. Typed numbers are plain text. Word's restart commands do not change them, so no menu option fixes a typed number. Delete those numbers and apply list formatting, as described below.

items: Typed numbers. You typed the digits yourself, so restart commands skip them.
List formatting. Word controls the number, so a restart command can change it.
Linked lists. The count carries on from an earlier list in the same document.
Lists with no Level 1 item above them. Microsoft's Q&A answer ties restart problems to this case.

blocks.text: Why Word carries the count over

Word tracks list numbers in sequences. Several lists can share one sequence, and the second list then carries on from the first. A Microsoft Q&A answer points to this when a list has no higher-level item to restart after it. Microsoft's own help page does not explain the internal cause, so treat this as the best available explanation, not an official one. The practical result is the same either way. You need a restart point, and a restart command or a structural fix gives you one.
Fix it with Restart at 1 in Word for Mac

Microsoft's help page gives the standard fix for this problem. It covers Word for Microsoft 365, Word 2024, Word 2021, Word 2019 and Word 2016. It does not name a Mac, and I did not open a Mac-specific page. The steps should match on a Mac, but menu names can differ. If a change goes wrong, press ⌘Z to undo it.

items: Click into the list so Word knows which list you mean.
Right-click the number of the item where the count should restart. With a trackpad, click with two fingers.
Choose Restart at 1 from the menu.
Scroll through the list and check that every item after it counts up.
If you need a different start value, choose Set Numbering Value and type the number you want.

blocks.title: Do not retype the numbers
blocks.text: Microsoft's page says to always use the command options, not manual edits. If Word loses track of manual edits, later list changes can cause problems in new places.
When Restart at 1 does nothing

Some people report that the command has no effect. In one Microsoft Q&A thread, a Word 365 user on Windows 10 found that Restart at 1 did nothing. Set Numbering Value had its Start new list and Continue from previous list options greyed out. If that happens to you, the list is probably tied to a list above it. Move to the structural fix below instead of repeating the same command.
Nest the list under a heading

The accepted answer in that thread, from a Microsoft MVP, is to make the numbered list Level 2 of a multilevel list. The Level 1 item above it can be a heading style or a Body Text paragraph. The list then restarts after each Level 1 paragraph. It takes a few more steps, but it gives Word a clear restart point.

items: Add a heading or Body Text paragraph directly above the list. This becomes Level 1.
Select the list items. Press Tab to move them to the second level.
Check that the first item shows the number you expect and that the count restarts after each Level 1 paragraph.
If your version uses a different level menu, ask Lazur to walk you through it.

blocks.text: Google Docs: restart or continue a list

Google Docs gives you explicit options for the start number. Double-click the first number of the list. Then choose Format > Bullets & numbering > List options > Restart numbering. Enter the new start number and click OK. To pick up an earlier list instead, select the first number and choose Continue previous numbering. That option works in Docs only, not in Slides. Google's help page shows no date, so check the menu names if they look different.
Pages on Mac: the fix is harder to find

Apple's Pages 15.4 guide does not document a Start from or Continue from Previous option. Its only numbering control sits in the Format sidebar, under Style, then Bullets & Lists, then Numbers. You can pick a number or letter sequence under Tiered Numbers there. The Start from fix you may find comes from an Apple Community thread about Pages 5.2.2 on a 2012 MacBook Pro. In that case, the answer was to choose Start from 11, and the poster confirmed it worked. Menus change between versions, so look in the Format sidebar first.

items: Select the list.
Open the Format sidebar and click Style.
Expand Bullets & Lists and check the numbering options.
If a Start from option appears, enter the number you want.

blocks.text: Ask Lazur for help without leaving the document

Hold ⌥⌘ and ask a question about what is on your screen. Lazur answers out loud. Ask where Restart at 1 is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to restart the list, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. Lazur does not click for you. Its answer comes from what is on screen, so check the menu yourself before you trust it.
Mistakes that make the problem return

The most common mistake is typing the right number over the wrong one. It looks fixed until you add or move an item. Then the typed number stays put while the rest of the list moves. The second mistake is copying a list from a web page or email. Copied lists bring their own numbering, and it can join a sequence you did not expect. Paste the text into a clean paragraph, then apply list formatting.
The third mistake is undoing too far. ⌘Z reverses one change at a time. Press it once, check the numbers, and press again only if you need to. That way you keep the fix you already made.
Check the fix before you send

items: Scroll the whole document, not just the list you fixed. A change in one place can move another list.
Add a test item in the middle of the list, then watch the numbers. Delete the test item afterwards.
Export or print a copy and check the numbers there.
Check again after a reviewer sends back edits.

blocks.text: When a shared file adds new problems

Reviewer edits can move list numbers too, so check again after you accept their changes. If you need to handle those changes first, read [how to accept or reject all tracked changes in Word for Mac](/for/writers/problems/word-mac-accept-reject-tracked-changes). A shared file also tempts people to fix numbers by hand. Ask them to use the list commands instead, so the problem does not come back.
If the document holds client or patient data

Follow your employer's rules before you use an AI tool on a file that holds client, patient or other regulated data. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your employer's policy still decides what you may share.
What the sources do not tell us

No study I found measures how often numbered lists restart at the wrong number. Nothing I found links this bug to grades, burnout or errors, so this page does not make those claims. The sources are vendor help pages and user reports, not controlled tests. The Word cause is inferred from one community answer. The Pages steps come from older threads. Test each fix on a copy of your file before you rely on it.
Where to go next

If the list also changed font or style after you pasted it, read [why pasted text changes fonts in Word for Mac](/for/writers/problems/word-mac-pasted-text-fonts-styles). For the wider set of Word habits, see [Word for writers on Mac](/for/writers/word). If you also work in Docs, the [Google Docs guide for writers](/for/writers/google-docs) covers the list commands there.

faq.question: Why does my numbered list start at the wrong number in Word?
faq.answer: Word can link your list to an earlier list in the same document. The second list then carries on from the first. Restart at 1 usually breaks that link. Typed numbers never restart on their own, so check whether the numbers are list formatting first.

faq.question: How do I restart a numbered list in Word for Mac?
faq.answer: Right-click the number where the count should start, then choose Restart at 1. Microsoft's help page describes this route. It does not name Mac, so check the menu names on your version. Press ⌘Z if the wrong list changes.

faq.question: Why does Restart at 1 do nothing in my document?
faq.answer: The list may be tied to a list above it, with no Level 1 item to restart from. In one Microsoft Q&A thread, that case also greyed out the options in Set Numbering Value. Add a heading or Body Text paragraph above the list, then make the list Level 2.

faq.question: Does this problem happen in Google Docs and Pages too?
faq.answer: Google Docs has a documented route: Format > Bullets & numbering > List options > Restart numbering. Pages has no documented restart option in Apple's current guide. Older community threads describe a Start from setting, so check the Format sidebar on your version.

faq.question: Is it safe to type the numbers by hand instead?
faq.answer: It looks fine at first, but typed numbers do not update when you add or move items. Microsoft advises against manual edits for this reason. Use list formatting, even if it takes a little longer.

faq.question: Can Lazur fix the numbering for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or edit files for you. It can draw a circle and a label around the right menu item, explain what it sees, or guide you one click at a time. You still make each click yourself.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur on a file with client or patient data?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules first. Lazur looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. The screenshot is sent to AI providers to answer and is not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

costs.title: Minutes that add up across a file
costs.text: Each wrong list is a small fix, but long files can hold several. The real cost is the repeated checking after each edit. You also lose time to retyping numbers, then fixing the retyping. I did not find data on how many minutes writers lose to this in total, so that cost stays unmeasured.

costs.title: Wages, if you bill by the hour
costs.text: The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the May 2025 median pay for secretaries and administrative assistants at $23.23 an hour. That job is not writing, so the figure is only a rough yardstick. If you bill by the hour, use your own rate to price the time. The number shows what formatting time can cost, not a fixed cost for writers.

costs.title: Readers may doubt the rest of the page
costs.text: A list that starts at the wrong number can make a reader think earlier steps are missing. In a manual, a form or a set of instructions, that confusion costs more than the fix. I did not find a study that measures this effect, so treat it as a reasoned risk, not a measured one.

costs.title: Manual fixes break again later
costs.text: Typed numbers break at the next edit. Microsoft warns that if Word loses track of manual edits, later list changes can cause problems. Each delayed fix adds another change to untangle later, and untangling takes longer than the first fix.

costs.title: Shared files spread the same error
costs.text: Reviewers and collaborators see the same wrong numbers. A reviewer may fix them by hand, which brings back the typed-number problem. Ask collaborators to use the list commands instead of manual edits.

causes.title: Lists share one numbering sequence
causes.text: Word can link several lists to one numbering sequence. When that happens, the second list carries on from the first instead of starting over. A Microsoft Q&A answer ties this to lists that have no higher-level item to restart them. Microsoft's help page does not explain the internal cause, so read this as the best available explanation. A restart command gives the list a new start, which is what you need.

causes.title: Numbers were typed by hand
causes.text: A typed number is plain text, not list formatting. Restart commands skip it, and Set Numbering Value cannot change it. Typed numbers also stay put when you add or remove items, so the list looks wrong after the next edit. Microsoft warns against manual edits for this reason. It says Word can lose track of them, and later list changes can then cause problems.

causes.title: Pasted lists bring their own numbers
causes.text: Copying from a web page, an email or another document can carry its numbering with it. The pasted list may join a sequence already in your file. Paste the text as plain text into a clean paragraph, then apply list formatting. Pasted text can also change fonts, which is a separate problem with its own fixes.

causes.title: No restart point above the list
causes.text: A list needs something above it that Word can restart from. In the Microsoft Q&A thread, a Level 1 paragraph, such as a heading style or Body Text, gave the restart point that fixed the count. Plain paragraphs at the same level may not do that. If your list has no heading above it, add one before you try more commands.

causes.title: Pages has no documented restart option
causes.text: Apple's current Pages guide does not list a Start from or Continue from Previous option. The only numbering control it documents sits in the Format sidebar, under Bullets & Lists. Older fixes come from community threads about Pages 5.2.2. Menus change between versions, so the fix may not be where those threads say.

causes.title: Google Docs needs an explicit choice
causes.text: Google Docs asks you to choose how the count should behave. Restart numbering starts a new count from a number you enter. Continue previous numbering picks up an earlier list. Each option answers a different question, so pick the one that matches what you want the list to do.

fixes.title: Right-click and choose Restart at 1
fixes.text: Select the list and right-click the number where the count should restart. Choose Restart at 1. Microsoft's help page gives this as the main route in Word. Scroll the list and check that every item after the restart point counts up correctly. If another list changed by mistake, press ⌘Z once and try again.

fixes.title: Use Set Numbering Value for a specific start
fixes.text: Right-click the number and choose Set Numbering Value when you need a start other than 1. Microsoft offers it as an alternative to Restart at 1. The Q&A thread shows Start new list and Continue from previous list as options in that dialog. If those options are greyed out for you, move on to the structural fix.

fixes.title: Nest the list under a Level 1 heading
fixes.text: Add a heading style or Body Text paragraph above the list, then make the list items Level 2 of a multilevel list. The list restarts after each Level 1 paragraph. This comes from the accepted answer in a Microsoft Q&A thread, written by an MVP. It worked for one Word 365 case, so test it on your own file.

fixes.title: Delete typed numbers and reapply the list
fixes.text: Remove every number you typed by hand, then apply list formatting again. Word then manages the numbers itself. Microsoft advises command options over manual edits, so this fix matches its advice. Check the first item after you reapply the list.

fixes.title: Google Docs: restart numbering
fixes.text: Double-click the first number of the list. Choose Format > Bullets & numbering > List options > Restart numbering. Enter the new start number and click OK. This path comes from Google's Docs Editors Help page. Menu names may move, so check the page if they look different.

fixes.title: Google Docs: continue previous numbering
fixes.text: Select the first number of the list, then choose Format > Bullets & numbering > List options > Continue previous numbering. Use this when the list should carry on an earlier count. The option is available in Docs only, not in Slides.

fixes.title: Pages: look for Start from in Bullets & Lists
fixes.text: Select the list. Open the Format sidebar, click Style, and expand Bullets & Lists. If a Start from option appears, enter the number you want. Apple's current guide does not document it, so treat this as a check for your version.

fixes.title: Paste as plain text, then reapply the list
fixes.text: If the list came from a web page, an email or another file, paste it into a clean paragraph as plain text. Then apply list formatting. This clears numbering you did not create. Pasted fonts and styles can also need a separate fix.

fixes.title: Rebuild the list in a new paragraph
fixes.text: If no fix holds, copy the item text into a new list and remove the old list afterwards. A new list usually starts without the old settings. Check the numbers after each change, so you know which step worked.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Find every list in the file
plan.text: Scroll the whole document and mark each list that looks wrong. Click the first number of each one. Decide which numbers are typed and which are list formatting. Keep a copy of the file before you change anything.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Test one fix on a copy
plan.text: Work on the copy. Try Restart at 1 on the first wrong list. If it does nothing, try nesting the list under a heading. Note which fix worked, so you can repeat it.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Fix the rest with the same method
plan.text: Apply the fix that worked to the remaining lists. Delete typed numbers and reapply list formatting where needed. Google Docs and Pages files need their own menu routes, covered above.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Check the whole file and export
plan.text: Add a test item in the middle of a list, watch the numbers, then delete it. Export or print a copy and check the numbers there. A printed or exported copy gives you a second look.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Set a habit for the next draft
plan.text: Apply list formatting from the start, and avoid typing numbers by hand. After each reviewer round, check the numbers again. If you tend to forget, ask Lazur to set a reminder.
